entries.title: Google Pixel Watch 5 Sale: Its Lowest Price Yet (2026)
entries.summary: Google’s latest smartwatch packs great new health and fitness features, and it’s already on sale ahead of Black Friday.
entries.content:
If you’ve been waiting for a good deal on Google’s latest smartwatch before you commit, you're in luck. The Google Pixel Watch 5 (the 41-mm model with Wi-Fi) is currently $300, down from $400, marking its lowest price yet. (The larger 45-mm model is also discounted, from $430 to $330.)

This early Black Friday sale means you don’t have to wait until the late-November holiday to score the worthwhile discount—and we recommend you don’t. Amazon, Best Buy, and the Google Store are all offering the 25 percent off deal, but I don’t know for how much longer. In other words, now is a great time to score this smartwatch for less.

A Record-Low Price

The Pixel Watch 5 is one of the best smartwatches available for Android users. It’s a refinement of an already brilliant wearable, with double the RAM and storage, plus an upgraded Qualcomm Snapdragon W5 Gen 2 processor that makes this edition 20 percent faster than its predecessor. The domed display is gorgeous, comfortable, and easy to read during workouts, and it provides meaningful upgrades for health and fitness tracking.

Beyond being able to track weights and reps, the new Strength Training experience includes a workout builder, audio cues, and rest times. You can build a custom routine in the Google Health app and have the watch guide you through each exercise, and incorporate Gemini AI by asking it to generate a workout based on a photo of your gym equipment. Speaking of Gemini, the Pixel Watch 5 supports certain offline tasks, such as starting a workout, which is nice if you like to leave your watch at home while you exercise.

Google’s new Health Guardian tools include features for monitoring insulin resistance trends, blood pressure trends, breathing emergencies (available only in select countries), and sleep breathing quality. The watch also retains useful features like ECG, skin temperature tracking, and loss-of-pulse detection. It comes with upgraded sleep tracking, too, with Google claiming 15 percent greater accuracy than the Pixel Watch 4.

Google estimates up to 40 hours of battery life, but mine only got to around 36 hours in testing before conking out. Fast charging is the real standout, though; just 15 minutes on the charger delivers up to 15 hours of use. If you’re like me and only remember to charge your watch 20 minutes before leaving the house, this is a lifesaver.

At its original $400 price, the Pixel Watch 5 is a pricey recommendation, especially since many of its software upgrades will also make their way to the previous generation. But at $300, it’s cheaper than the latest Apple Watch Series 12 and other high-end smartwatches. This is the lowest price I’ve seen for the Pixel Watch 5, so if you’ve been eyeing it, there’s little reason to wait for Black Friday.

entries.title: How a Contractor’s Claude Agent Got Into the Pentagon
entries.summary: This week on Uncanny Valley, we also discuss Anthropic’s IPO filing and the volunteers gearing up to counter ICE at the midterms.
entries.content:
This week on Uncanny Valley, Brian Barrett, Leah Feiger, and Zoë Schiffer dive into our scoop on how a defense contractor connected Claude Code to a secure Department of Defense system. We also discuss the green, yellow, and red flags we see in Anthropic’s IPO filing—and why it’s a test not just for the AI industry but for the entire US economy—and how volunteers nationwide are preparing for ICE agents potentially showing up at polling sites in the midterms.

Articles mentioned in this episode:

  • A Defense Contractor Gave Their Personal AI Agent Access to a Secure Pentagon System
  • The Anthropic S-1 Filing Is Also an AI Doomsday Primer
  • What’s Worth More Than Cash in San Francisco Real Estate? Anthropic Stock
  • Massive Groups of Volunteers Are Ready to Face Down ICE at the Polls

You can follow Brian Barrett on Bluesky at @brbarrett, Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer, and Leah Feiger on Bluesky at @leahfeiger. Write to us at [email protected].

How to Listen

You can always listen to this week’s podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here’s how:

If you’re on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “uncanny valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Transcript

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Brian Barrett: Welcome to the WIRED’s Uncanny Valley. I’m Brian Barrett, executive editor.

Zoë Schiffer: I’m Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor.

Leah Feiger: And I’m Leah Feiger, director of politics and science.

Zoë Schiffer: This week, Anthropic has officially filed to go public. There is a lot going on in the hundreds of pages that the company submitted as part of its S-1 filing, from staggering earnings and losses, to warnings of AI’s existential threat. Obviously, we’re talking about Anthropic here. We’ll discuss our key takeaways and why this IPO is kind of high stakes, not just for the AI industry, but honestly the entire US economy.

Leah Feiger: We’re also bringing you a scoop about how a defense contractor plugged Anthropic’s Claude into a secure Department of Defense system, in what’s really one of the most outlandish uses of AI in the government we’ve seen so far.

Brian Barrett: And the midterms are right around the corner, just a few days away. Massive groups of volunteers all over the country are already getting ready to protect their communities from the potential that ICE officers show up at the polls. We’ll get into how grassroots efforts like these are a reflection of a deeply uncertain election cycle.

Zoë Schiffer: So on Monday, we learned that Anthropic finally pulled the trigger and publicly filed for its IPO. This has been highly anticipated for a bunch of reasons. Anthropic is expected to raise more money in its IPO than any company in history, and it would be the first major US company focused solely on building AI software to go public. To give you a sense of the scale that we’re talking about, the company’s valuation went from $183 billion a little over a year ago to $965 billion in its most recent round, and some expect that it could be worth close to $2 trillion once it starts trading. So the filing basically gives us the first real look inside Anthropic’s business because it’s a private company right now. It doesn’t have to report a bunch of stuff. And the numbers are pretty extreme in both directions, billions of dollars in revenue and even more billions in losses, and hundreds of billions that the company has already committed to compute. Because there’s a ton to unpack in this paperwork, I thought it would be fun to divide it into green flags, yellow flags, and red flags that we saw from the filing. What do you guys think?

Brian Barrett: Yes.

Leah Feiger: I’m astounded by how much money is at play here. This is, yes.

Brian Barrett: What flag, Leah? What flag is that?

Leah Feiger: I don’t know.

Zoë Schiffer: For the sake of the economy, it’s green.

Brian Barrett: Great. Green flag.

Leah Feiger: For the sake of the economy, it’s green. This is so much money, guys. Sue me, but the only thing I can think of right now is that article that WIRED ran a couple of months ago about how people were selling their homes in the Bay Area with the promise of Anthropic stock post-IPO. And I remember at the time I was like, "How close are we to this?" And Zoe said, "Oh, they’re going to make so much money."

Brian Barrett: Is it fair to say, Zoë, I feel like having the financials out there, yes, they’re losing money hand over fist, but the financials I think are better than people were expecting maybe. At least, it feels like they put a lot of concerns to rest, not all of them, but this is a real business. This is a business that is growing. It’s doing all the things you would want a business to do.

Zoë Schiffer: Yes, I think absolutely. So its revenue hit $16.3 billion in the first half of 2026, and it’s grown more than 14 fold from the same period last year. I think we have to go back to 2022 and remember that when ChatGPT came on the scene, it wasn’t even apparent that AI would have a real enterprise application. This was a consumer app that didn’t have really any business case for it. And it wasn’t until Anthropic came on the scene years later, it rolled out Claude Code that we started to really see like, oh no, there’s a viable business and actually the majority of the money is going to come from other businesses using their coding product. This is also, I think, a key difference that you hear from insiders between Dario and Sam. People very close to Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, will say he wakes up every single day and says, "Enterprise code." That is the thing he cares about. And that’s because that’s the thing that makes money for these businesses. Whereas I think the perception from some is that OpenAI is a little more scattered and all over the place. And I think you can see that in the numbers.

Brian Barrett: So they are leaning in. They have Claude code, huge success, enterprise code, huge success. I will say, to introduce a yellow flag, of that revenue that you talked about, very impressive revenue over $60 billion, nearly half of it came from three tech companies cloud marketplaces. So they are pretty heavily reliant on a small number of companies which are also competitors. It is this sort of tangled nest of reliances in this industry that feels, I think Anthropic didn’t put it as one of its major risk factors. We can talk about the risk factors in a second because that was my favorite section, but it does feel like, where’s the moat? Is there enough of one given how much they’re relying on a handful of companies that are also developing their own AI, other AI products are getting better, open source products, open weight products are out there. How yellow is that flag?

Zoë Schiffer: I think it’s yellow. It’s not surprising that a polyamorous worker cooperative would be incestuous in its business dealings. I was not shocked by that information. And it’s not unusual for a small percentage of spenders to have an out-sized impact on a company’s revenue. I think there was another number that Ramp put out recently, 80 percent of revenue for both Anthropic and OpenAI comes from about the top 1 percent of AI spenders. So the companies that are spending the most account for the vast majority of the company’s revenues. But it is a vulnerability, because if there’s a pullback and those companies start spending less, Anthropic is exposed. But another, I don’t know where to put this flag. I think it’s green. They were transparent about some of the risks involved in the IPO, some of the existential risks of AI generally. This is probably my favorite part in the whole thing. “Concerns have been raised ... That sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed and safeguarded appropriately, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

Leah Feiger: Incredible stuff.

Zoë Schiffer: The use of the passive voice in this S-1, concerns have been raised by Dario to be so for real.

Brian Barrett: Internally by Anthropic, I will say too, the phrase existential risk comes up three times. It’s twice existential risk to humanity, once existential risk to society. So in that scenario, presumably there are still humans, they have just abandoned any semblance of a social contract.

Zoë Schiffer: Great.

Brian Barrett: Zoë, I love that this was a green flag for you, the fact that they’re so openly-

Leah Feiger: She’s a transparent lady.

Brian Barrett: And to be clear, they have been shouting this since they started that AI could kill everybody. This is not new for them. What I thought was interesting, and I’ll call it a red flag, red flag for humanity, yellow flag for Anthropic, green flag for me because I love to talk about it. So the same thing that they cite as most likely to cause the end of human life on earth, is the thing that they also cite as one of their primary competitive advantages. And that is recursive self-improvement. So that’s where an AI model can improve itself. And they’re saying on the one hand, if AI models keep getting better at improving themselves, and can eventually improve themselves to the point where humans don’t even need to look at it, closing the loop where AI just gets better, and makes AI better, and makes AI better to the point where we don’t even understand what AI is doing anymore, but gosh, it’s good and it’s making a lot of money, that’s the scenario in which AI is powerful enough to maybe end the world. But it’s also, Anthropic notes also we’re really good at that. We’re investing a lot of money in that. That’s how we’re going to get ahead.

Zoë Schiffer: And how relatable is that? Who among us doesn’t have a shadow side that is equally augmented by the power that that shadow side gives you?

Leah Feiger: To be clear, and WIRED covered this, as did basically everyone. When former Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned and said it was because Anthropic could bring about the end of the world, he specifically cited curbing RSI at the top of his list. This is the whole ballgame.

Brian Barrett: Yes. And then the industry in general is very ... I think this is probably too extreme, but Bernie Sanders has a bill out there, and Ro Khanna has a separate bill that say, "Hey, let’s just ban recursive self-improvement. Let’s just say we’re not doing that." I will say one little note is that the risk factors is the longest section of the prospectus. It’s 94 pages, I believe. So they could have just said, "We have a shadow side and saved everybody.

Zoë Schiffer: I would’ve understood.

Brian Barrett: A lot of trouble."

Leah Feiger: Can we talk about a red flag that I haven’t gotten a great answer on yet, and I kind of need you to explain this to me like I’m a toddler? The compute bill, all of this technology costs so much money. I don’t personally feel like I have an understanding of where the limit is, how you do not spend enough to use all of your money and also spend enough to not put yourself out of business and end your technology forever. Perhaps I do not understand compute in its entirety or where it comes from, but all of this together, this is just so much. Tell me.

Zoë Schiffer: It is so much. I’m not going to pretend that I understand it. The scale of what we’re talking about is, again, totally unprecedented. You get a lot of railroad analogies when you start talking about this stuff, but I will say that one key difference is that unlike the railroad companies, which were operating on slightly thinner margins, these are still very well-funded and rich companies. And so yes, they’re investing a ton in compute, and they expect that that compute will be needed. So far it is, and they expect that to continue to rise. I personally think that that is a viable argument, but of course the flip side is like, well, if growth starts to seriously slow down, and they’re left holding the bill for all of this compute that they’ve committed to, a lot of the contracts that Anthropic has signed, they can’t get out of. That’s going to be really bad, and it’s going to be bad not just for Anthropic, but for the entire US economy.

Leah Feiger: They call it their most significant operating cost, in quotes.

Zoë Schiffer: Yes, absolutely.

Brian Barrett: I think significant too, that unlike say SpaceX, unlike Meta, other companies that are heavily invested in AI, a lot of what Anthropic is doing is basically leasing compute. They are not building as much. They are contracting out. So on the one hand, that maybe frees them from long-term obligations on these massive properties. On the other hand, obviously it’s sort of, to Zoë’s point, they’re contracts they can’t get out of. They are committed to these contracts, and they don’t really control their own destiny in that regard, especially when the compute is very competitive now. Getting access to compute has been really, really hard. It’s getting harder, especially as finance companies are less inclined to provide the debt, to support the debt to pay for all these infrastructure costs. One thing I wanted to add really quick is that they do say in the prospectus, I just need to call this out, that the company needs to make forward investments that will seem, "irresponsibly large," at first, which if Zoë found the shadow self relatable, I found this relatable because it’s what I tell my family every time I order DoorDash.

Zoë Schiffer: I know.

Brian Barrett: It’s going to be irresponsibly large at first glance.

Leah Feiger: But will pay off eventually.

Brian Barrett: Yeah.

Zoë Schiffer: Absolutely.

Leah Feiger: I want to move us over to talk about a massive story that WIRED published today that also has to do with Anthropic’s Claude. WIRED’s Victoria Elliot reported today all about a security incident at the Department of Defense caused by a contractor who connected a secure centralized system, one used by multiple intelligence agencies, to their personal account for Claude Code, Anthropic’s commercial AI coding agent. The contractor works for the global consulting firm Accenture, and according to sources, the agent sent information about the DOD system along with login credentials, to a high-risk third-party website. And it ran inside the DOD network sources tell us for two months before anyone caught on.

Brian Barrett: No.

Zoë Schiffer: Red flag. Red flag.

Brian Barrett: Red flag. Red flag.

Leah Feiger: Really to start us off, and I want to get into these details and everyone should go read this on wired.com, but I think the overarching thing that I really want to get across here is we have not seen this before. This is a massive, massive example of an AI agent in theory wreaking havoc, or even just having access to government systems without people’s knowledge of that.

Brian Barrett: First of all, huge scoop by Tori. Major credit to her. Really, really well done. I’m surprised there was not a system in place to catch this. I’m surprised that it was allowed to happen in the first place. It feels like there are multiple levels of failings here, and I think speaks to just sort of this is the DoD, this is happening, I assume, at all kinds of organizations as people become more reliant on agents to do literally whatever for them.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. God, those people. Leah, my question for you, and then I want to give my take, is that we don’t know that anything nefarious was going on. This contractor was trying to use Claude to write code and deploy it.

Leah Feiger: Yes. So this isn’t a massive hacking attempt.

Zoë Schiffer: I think that’s more interesting though.

Leah Feiger: I agree. I agree. It’s the idea that there was access at all.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah. The thing that it reminds me of is a really popular product in Silicon Valley, maybe everywhere right now, is this recording tool and transcription tool called Granola. Basically, it’s this thing that connects to your calendar. When you have a meeting, it automatically starts recording. The result of that is that in many states, you’re illegally recording people all the time. And it’s become such a norm in Silicon Valley that everyone’s just thrown up their hands and been like, "Whatever. I guess this is just what we’re doing now." And this reminds me of that. I think that people are so used to having agents do things for them, or using Claude Code where they would’ve previously written and deployed code by hand, that they’re not as aware that what they’re doing is breaking norms, rules, laws.

Brian Barrett: I just want to quickly confirm, because I Googled it just now, California is a two-party consent state. If that’s useful to anyone out there who’s using Granola.

Zoë Schiffer: It’s fully illegal. It’s fully illegal.

Brian Barrett: It’s fully illegal. You are breaking the law.

Leah Feiger: I really wish that you could see my slack-jawed open-faced right now, the fact that that exists. But back to the Accenture of it all, back to the DoD of it all, this system that this Claude agent had access to, the centralized system contains controlled unclassified information. So it’s CUI, it’s considered to be sensitive, but not to be released to the public without review. The issue though is that the way that different pieces of this information from this system and other parts that the system has access to, can be combined to create classified information. Does that make sense?

Brian Barrett: Yeah.

Zoë Schiffer: Unfortunately, yeah.

Leah Feiger: To spell this out a little bit more, this can include information about critical infrastructure across the US, nuclear submarine propulsion, vulnerabilities to chemical and biological terrorism. This is not casual stuff that they had access to. The source aware of the incident who requested anonymity to speak to Tori said to her, "It puts all the data that’s in there at risk. If the third party software was compromised, there could be somebody out there with the ability to log into a secure environment without anyone knowing. It’s 100 percent a national security threat and could cause irreparable harm." This is serious. So the Accenture employee who was alleged to have connected this secure production environment to their personal Claude account to allow this agent to write and deploy code is also breaking another rule technically, because Claude is currently barred from being used by DoD staff.

Brian Barrett: Oh yeah.

Zoë Schiffer: Were we ever so young?

Leah Feiger: Ever so young. This is a Mad Lib story. This is a Mad Lib story, to automate the process the contractor gave their login credentials. The agent wasn’t just writing code, but committing it, meaning that it was saving the code to the system on the employee’s behalf. And also they had to connect to the internet, so some of these things were air-gapped.

Zoë Schiffer: Do we know what accountability looks like here? What has happened to the employee, what Accenture or the DoD are doing in the wake of this?

Leah Feiger: That is a great question. Despite the security risks, sources told WIRED that Accenture employees did not really treat the incident as super severe or urgent.

Brian Barrett: Good, good, good.

Leah Feiger: Yep. Good, good, good. So when we reached out to the Department of Defense, a spokesperson there told us that, "The department does not comment on the status of its networks or systems." And on Accenture’s end, their spokesperson said that they "take all concerns seriously. These allegations were thoroughly and independently investigated and found to be without merit. We fully complied with our legal and contractual obligations." When pressed though, Accenture didn’t offer clarification on who conducted the investigation, or dispute that there had been what could be characterized as an incident. I have to say, this isn’t the first time that Accenture has had a bit of an issue recently. Earlier this month, the FBI found that an Accenture contractor did not patch a vulnerability that led to the hacking group Shiny Hunters getting access to all of the FBI data. I don’t know if you guys remember that fun story. So lots of things happening here. So many different questions, for me at least, brought up about the use of personal AI agents when it comes to the workspace, contractors and government and what they have access to, what they have to reveal to the government at what time. There’s a lot here that fell in the cracks, and like I said earlier, Mad Libs, Mad Libs of a bad situation just really gone awry.

Brian Barrett: It feels like the use of AI agents in general, it’s a shortcut. It’s like I want to take a shortcut to whatever it is I’m doing. Sometimes that’s for great reasons. Zoë, you’ve given over 80 percent of your life to agents and you’re thriving, but there are some situations where you really shouldn’t take any kind of shortcut, especially not a shortcut that you can’t really control that’s going to be touching sensitive documents. Yeah, it’s inexcusable. I assume not the last time we’re going to hear about something like this. Well, in other news, the midterms are officially a week away and early voting already underway in lots of states. You may have already voted as you’re listening to this, power to you if so. One of the questions hanging over these elections though has nothing to do with who’s on the ballot. It’s who’s going to be at the polling stations. For the last six months, President Trump and his allies have declined to rule out the possible deployment of ICE agents to voting sites during the midterms, even though that would be illegal under federal law, has not really stopped him before in various scenarios. This week, WIRED’s David Gilbert spoke to a dozen people or so taking part in a nationwide effort to get ready for that possibility. They’re in towns and cities across the country, and they are people who see the presence of ICE at the polls as an existential threat to democracy. They’ve built massive networks of people to do a couple different things. The overall goal though is to A, document what ICE is doing and B, spread the word about rights to voters. So if you do go to the polls and you see ICE there, you know how to respond and react. Great that people are planning for this. Leah, I’m curious, how much of a likelihood or inevitability do you think this is going to be? ICE showing up at the polls and kind of disrupting ... I guess their very presence is disruptive, right? I think so it’s really just how likely do you think it is that they actually show up?

Leah Feiger: A really good question and one that I’m honestly changing my mind on every few days. Recently, the Trump administration has indicated that they will not be sending ICE to the polls. Like you said, the last couple of months have been the exact opposite of that. And then you also have DHS and other random government accounts posting about how they are apprehending illegal voters as we speak. So there’s some mixed messaging that’s clearly happening right now. And in the middle of that, these organizations have stepped in to say, "OK, here’s our plan should this happen." Simultaneously, I think there’s just a lot of fear. Do I think that every single polling station is going to have that? No. Do I think that fear about it is probably going to dissuade some people from voting? Yeah. Yeah, I do. This isn’t forcing you to stand in a line for hours on end, which to be clear, also bad. This is the threat that you are going to be thrown in a facility and never see your family or your home ever again. This is massive. This is what ICE tactics have been in the past. So applying it to this situation, very, very scary. Will it happen? I think we’re probably going to see some of it. I think it’s going to happen in a couple of different ways, whether that’s agents standing near polling places that act as an intimidation to certain voters. Are they interfering or not? Tough to say. I think that there’s also going to be a lot of probably false accusations of this as well. We don’t know. But the possibility for misinformation, I say misinformation, not disinformation, because people are just going to be spreading things around that they haven’t perhaps verified because of fear, because of what the Trump administration has been promising and has done in so many communities across the US over this past year, is very real and very scary.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I think that’s exactly right. I think fear is the point and confusion is the point. I live in California. We already have multiple examples of people we know who probably won’t be able to participate in the way that they normally would have because the possibility that ICE would be there is just too scary. And so whether or not they’re actually at a particular polling place, it might not matter. And I think if they are at a few, I think we can expect to see a kind of flood the zone where those images start to go everywhere. And in some cases it’s people trying to warn other people, but I would expect that also in a lot of cases it might be just people trying to spread fear and dissuade people from getting out to vote.

Leah Feiger: And that’s where some of these organizations come in that David talked to. You have 614 ICE Watch, you have groups like the Common Cause, ACLU, Indivisible that have been training their teams and these massive groups of volunteers to actually be able to track examples of ICE at the polls, and to share verified information with their networks, which include people that have been working in democratic spaces for a very, very long time. So that is in place. It’s going to be about wading through the noise.

Brian Barrett: I think 614 ICE Watch is a really good example because they’re focusing their efforts in Columbus, Ohio, home to a large Somali American community that was targeted by an ICE operation last year. This is a community that’s really rattled by ICE and is really affected by ICE. And so even just knowing, look, there’s someone here who’s looking out for you. There’s a group of people here who, if something does happen, they’ll be there. Whether ICE shows up or not, it may encourage people to go to the polls when they otherwise might have stayed home for the reason Zoë was just talking about. So even just it’s sort of a preemptive strike that I think is really great. It’s great that they’re doing it and I hope that it is effective. I hope people still are able to go out and vote.

Leah Feiger: Absolutely. And to Zoë’s point, because it’s not me if I don’t bring this into some of the political machinations behind the scenes as well, I think that this is, and the fear around it, and the discourse around it and all of this is really just heightened by the fact that Republicans are getting trounced in the polls, you guys, absolutely trounced. WIRED senior correspondent Hugo Lowell put out a newsletter this week all about how Republicans, the week before midterms, are doubling down their spending and resources on Senate races in states that are traditionally deep red. We’re talking Kansas. I’m sorry. In what world is that up for grabs? It’s not even to say that these elections are necessarily, for sure absolutely going to go Democrat. It’s that they’re frightened. It’s that the polls are way closer than they should be. And so all of this aside, what’s a great way for the Republican Party to start pointing fingers, oh, this election has been impacted by voting of ’illegal immigrants.’ Oh, we’re going to send ICE. ICE should be there X, Y, and Z. So it’s all of this together has created an environment of real uncertainty. It’s a very apt time to have the elections, days after Halloween. I am spooky, spooky all around.

Brian Barrett: Wait, Leah, just because it’s our last recording before the midterms, what is your prediction? How are you going? House, Senate, who’s taking it?

Leah Feiger: Dems are going to take the House. Senate is still a toss-up to me.

Brian Barrett: Red flag. Red flag. You got to pick, Leah.

Leah Feiger: Hey, that’s pretty good. I feel like I gave a good guess there.

Brian Barrett: All right. All right. Coming up after the break, we’ll share our WIRED/TIRED picks for the week. Stay with us.

Leah Feiger: It’s time for our WIRED/TIRED segment. As usual, whatever is new and cool is WIRED, and whatever passé thing we’re over is TIRED. Let’s see what we’ve got. Zoë, I’ve heard you got a good one this week.

Zoë Schiffer: Yeah, I dedicate it to my dear friend, Leah Feiger. As you are well aware, as everyone is well aware, the billboards in San Francisco talking about AI, I think are insane. They are not legible as any part of the English language, unclear who they’re talking to or why they’re talking at all. I am sick of them personally. It’s complete nonsense and confusing. Yes.

Leah Feiger: It’s gobbledygook. Driving through San Francisco is hell.

Zoë Schiffer: Yes, it is. In contrast, The Row took out a double page ad in FT. I know. I was like, "You know what I’m talking about." A few weeks ago, and it was just a William Eggleston photo, just like a landscape photo, literally no text or anything. And I was like, "Way to zig while everyone else is zagging." It just spoke to their taste and aesthetic. Thought it was so fucking classy. I loved it.

Leah Feiger: I’m so with you. Talking of ads in unexpected places, did you see that Coterie—I don’t know if I’m pronouncing that correctly—the diaper company? They took out an ad in Golf Digest as a way to target the uneven mental load in parenting. I loved it.

Zoë Schiffer: I do like that.

Leah Feiger: And it’s also a great ad. Yeah. Wow, some good ads. All right, that’s a really good WIRED. Big fan. Any TIREDs for you?

Zoë Schiffer: The hideous billboards, that we discussed.

Leah Feiger: That makes sense. Absolutely yes. Brian, how about you?

Brian Barrett: Sure. I’ll be quick. I think my WIRED, not because of the thing itself, but it’s the only place I can squeeze in some consumer tech news in this podcast. Apple is releasing their first touchscreen Mac. They said they’d never do it. They finally did it. I personally don’t care about a touchscreen Mac. I will never buy one. I don’t have much use for one, but I like that they’re at least doing something a little bit different, and I like that they have gone back on their word. That’s fun. That’s WIRED. And my TIRED is going to be, you all may remember when Chris Nolan’s The Odyssey came out, big deal, great movie, a lot of fun. Elon Musk and associates: not fans, because it was too woke in various ways. So he promised that Grok would make an unwoke Odyssey, and by god, they did it.

Leah Feiger: Thank god.

Brian Barrett: They released the first chapter of chapter, whatever, seven-minute snippet of The Odyssey, and boy, is it terrible. It’s extremely bad. I don’t think it’s woke, at least. I think they succeeded on that front, but not super watchable either. So that’s TIRED for me.

Leah Feiger: That’s pretty good.

Brian Barrett: Leah, what about you?

Leah Feiger: My TIRED this week is, this is so boring of me, but election disinformation about quote unquote, “illegal voters.” This is a thing that I’m going to talk about for the rest of my life, the number of people voting who are not allowed to do so in the US is such a teeny, teeny, tiny number so as to have certainly never once influenced an election. And I am so TIRED that day in, day out, election in, election out, I am still talking about this. It’s tiring. I’m over it. Go read all of our reporting on wired.com about how wrong it is. My WIRED for this week is entirely unconnected. Halloween is on a Saturday. Halloween is not going to be on a Saturday again for many years. Really fun. I have some good plans. I hope you do too. I can’t wait to see all your costumes. Brian, Zoë, send your children’s costumes.

Zoë Schiffer: Oh yeah. I was going to say I’m an adult. I don’t wear costumes, but my kids, absolutely.

Brian Barrett: We are still nailing those down, but as soon as we get it.

Leah Feiger: DoorDash, Brian.

Brian Barrett: I will send it right over.

Leah Feiger: Perfect.

Zoë Schiffer: That’s our show for today. We’ll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was mixed by Pran Bandi, who’s also our New York studio engineer. It was fact-checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer and Katie Drummond is WIRED’s global editorial director.

entries.title: A Supply Chain Attack Put Malicious Anthropic Claude Extensions on Thousands of Devices
entries.summary: Thanks to a lucky break, flawed code in a tainted Claude extension prevented the attacker from fully worming their way into some 5,000 developer machines.
entries.content:
The AI software-development platform Cursor, which is owned by SpaceX, had a malicious Anthropic Claude Code extension for Windows, macOS, and Linux live in its integrated development environment extension marketplace for roughly 11 hours on Thursday. The company says the rogue extension was downloaded by “at most 5,000 users.” Cursor briefly shut down the extension marketplace while it investigated the situation, which the company says did not impact any other extensions.

The tainted extension was designed with a backdoor to give attackers access to victim devices—the type of implant that malicious hackers often use as a stepping stone to deeper control inside a target network. Cursor published remediation steps on Thursday for the roughly 5,000 affected targets. A saving grace of the situation, though, was a flaw in the malware's design that blocked it from fully establishing itself on the vast majority of targets.

“Everyone was so lucky here, this was potentially a really dangerous foothold for an attacker,” says Calum Hall, cofounder and CEO of the detection firm Phorion, the first researchers to spot the malicious extension after detecting it on a customer's Mac.

What is still unclear is how the malicious extension made its way into the Cursor marketplace at all. Some researchers initially speculated that it came from a compromised Anthropic system. But Cursor said in its Thursday security alert that “these malicious versions of the extension were not developed by Anthropic.”

Felix Rieseberg, a member of Anthropic's technical staff, posted on X on Friday: “We’re working with Cursor on this incident, but it wasn’t a compromise of Anthropic’s systems or employee laptops. A malicious actor used access to Cursor’s marketplace to publish a tampered copy of the Claude Code extension, which we didn’t build or publish. The versions on our official channels are not affected and this only impacts Cursor users.”

David Dworken, who works on security at Anthropic, posted on X shortly after, explaining that “this did not involve a compromise of any Anthropic systems … We were not involved with building, publishing, or hosting this.”

Cursor did not return WIRED's request for comment about how the malicious upload happened and whether it was the result of a breach at Cursor.

entries.title: People Are Creating ‘Survival Guides’ to Cope With the ‘AO3 Apocalypse’
entries.summary: The fanfic site could be down for weeks due to a “security incident.” Users are not taking it well.
entries.content:
In a major blow to both the terminally online and the criminally horny, the fan fiction website Archive of Our Own (AO3) has temporarily shut down due to a “security incident,” according to an update posted on the site.

On October 29, an admin for AO3 posted that the website was “down for maintenance.” The statement said that it could take up to four weeks for service to be fully restored, though it was possible the site would be back up in a “degraded state” sooner, with some of its features disabled.

Though the original statement did not specify the reasons for the closure, subsequent updates said that a “security incident” had taken place, though “we are still in the early stages of response [and] determining its scope.” While the statement said that AO3 did not believe that its user database had been stolen, it urged users to exercise caution and change their passwords for the site.

Run by the Organization for Transformative Works, a nonprofit dedicated to preserving fandom communities on the internet, AO3 was founded in 2007 in part due to concerns about censorship and corporate interests overtaking fandom spaces. The website has 11 million users, according to a 2026 press release, and hosts more than 18 million original works. The explosive popularity of the gay hockey romance Heated Rivalry TV series generated a surge of new interest last year, resulting in the publication of tens of thousands of stories featuring the show’s main characters, Shane Hollander and Ilya Rozanov, on the platform.

Those reliant on AO3 for their daily dose of Destiel- or Dramione-inspired smut are not taking the news well. “No ao3 for possibly 4 weeks SOMEONE DO SOMETHING,” one Heated Rivalry fan account posted on X, tagging not just AO3 itself but also the official X accounts for the FBI, the CIA, and, for some reason, Uber Support. Other fans are compiling Google Docs of links to downloaded stories, touting them as “survival guides” for the “AO3 apocalypse” and organizing them by fictional character pairings, or ships. (Be warned, however: One such doc is difficult to load due to “heavy traffic” on the file.)

Others commented on the timing of the outage, pointing out that it coincides with “No Nut November,” the internet-based challenge that encourages people to abstain from masturbation throughout the month. “AO3 taking no nut november a little too seriously,” one person wrote.

A representative for the Organization for Transformative Works did not immediately respond to a request for comment. But the chaos inspired by the site’s shutdown underscores the prominence of fan fiction in everyday lives, driving mainstream publishing trends and generating hundreds of millions of views. It also serves as the engine for the burgeoning vertical video industry, with streaming platforms constantly scouring fan fiction websites for works to adapt.

“All life forms dependent on AO3 are literally withering right now,” one fan wrote. “This is our 9/11.”

entries.title: I Spent 30 Minutes With Apple’s CEO. Now I Know Why John Ternus Got the Job
entries.summary: Apple doesn’t need fixing, and it doesn’t want drama. Its new leader is a “product guy” who bleeds six colors.
entries.content:
The brief ceremony introducing the new Macbook Pro this week was as low-key as the presenter, Apple’s new CEO John Ternus. He stepped onto the low stage at a Los Angeles event space with zero fanfare, said hi, and queued up a video showing the first touchscreen Mac. Then he released the modest crowd of journalists and creators to get hands-on with the new laptop and roam between eye-popping demos of music producers, filmmakers, photographers, and fashion designers using the laptop. Ternus, who at 51 is on the younger side of Apple’s top management, has been CEO for less than two months. But this launch and a series of other recent announcements have made one thing clear. With this new guy—if a 25-year Apple veteran could be considered new—it’s all about the products. Perhaps fittingly, the biggest noise of the presentation came when Ternus revealed that the new device restores the illumination to the Apple logo. Maybe that’s a symbol that in the age of AI, Apple is beaming out the message that hardware still rules.

A few minutes after the presentation, I sat down with Ternus, for the second time in two days. Steve Jobs used to grant me an audience after his famous keynotes, too. Ternus isn’t Jobs, of course, nor is he supposed to be. But who is he?

I first met Ternus in 2015, when I spent a day with him at Apple’s Input Design Lab, a testing facility in Cupertino. He’d risen to VP for Mac, iPad, Ecosystem, and Audio Engineering, and he struck me as affable and knowledgeable. (He spent four years right out of college at a virtual reality company, but he’s been at Apple ever since.) The peg to my story at the time was how this unknown manager conducted a Javert-like investigation to fix the weird sound a redesigned mouse made when sliding on a table.

That attention to detail was a legacy of Jobs’ perfectionism, which Tim Cook sustained as the next CEO. In the decade when Ternus overlapped with Jobs, he says he had only “a handful of interactions” with the founder. “But I've always felt like sort of a student of Steve's teachings,” Ternus said. “And then being able to work very closely with Tim, I’ve been very lucky.”

Ternus has so far been defined by his product prowess. “John innately has a great sense for great products, and that’s what Apple is,” says Greg Joswiak, Apple’s SVP of worldwide marketing and a 40-year company veteran. “You can’t teach that.” In one sense Ternus’ ascension is similar to that of Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, another lifer promoted to the top post. But Nadella was called upon to fix a broken organization, while Apple has been on a multi-decade run. Ternus is explicit that he will be an engine of continuity. That word is key to his selection, and above all explains why Tim Cook and the rest of Apple’s board was so comfortable with the choice.

The extent to which Ternus is a deep Apple insider became clear when I probed him on his views on being a corporate leader. I asked him which non-Apple CEOs he admires, and he was stumped. “I haven't really thought about that,” he said. I asked whether any business books had an impact on him. “Not really,” he said. “Of course I’ve read books, but there's so much to be learned from the people I get to work with.” Indeed, every time I tried to pin down Ternus on what mark he wants to make at Apple, he deflected the question and told me how he will continue Apple’s commitment to internal collaboration.

Ternus’ key collaborator is probably Johny Srouji, the architect of the company’s custom silicon, an initiative that’s driven many of the company’s innovations in the past decade. Srouri says that their relationship will be even closer, as Apple has merged its hardware engineering and technology organizations with Srouji at the top, reporting to Ternus. “John is going to be a great CEO,” he said. “He's a product guy at heart, but Apple's secret weapon is the DNA, the culture, which is not going to change. Remember, John has been here for 25 years. It’s not like he's going to come and everything's going to be different.”

Being Apple’s CEO encompasses much more than products—there’s a $100 billion business in services, a huge infrastructure, and the general mishegoss of running a giant corporation. I asked Ternus what it’s like to take on a massively expanded portfolio. “One of the amazing privileges of this job is getting to learn so many new things,” he said. “I have been and will continue to learn and go deeper into different areas. But, you know, I do love product. I'm super passionate about it.”

Like it or not, the CEO of a $4 trillion company has to be involved in policy and politics. It has been widely reported that as executive chair, Cook will still conduct some of Apple’s high-level policy duties, including the equivalent of stuffing gold-plated binkies in the presidential mouth. Ternus implies that the reality is more nuanced. “Tim is available to help wherever I ask him, and it's great to have him in that role,” he said. “He obviously has a ton of relationships he's developed over the years, and of course, I'm building new relationships in this role as well.” One relationship he has yet to build: the president. Ternus has yet to meet Donald Trump.

Then there’s the one thing that could possibly disrupt the way Apple has run its business for the past 50 years. Ternus is taking over the company during what may be the biggest technological shift ever. I suggested to Ternus that history may judge him on how he handles AI. I spelled out for him a couple of narratives people spin about Apple. One is that Apple has been hobbled by a failure to develop its AI product Siri, and even after an update it’s still in catch-up mode. The other is that Apple is smart to avoid the high cost of developing a frontier model and that the strategy of organically putting AI into its products, with a focus on privacy, will pay off in the long run.

“Everyone has an opinion—I really like where we’re at,” he said. “I would hope people recognize that the work we do is building incredible products that make their lives better. We’re absolutely going to leverage AI to do that. We don't want to ship AI for AI's sake. When we're doing it right, people won’t have to think about whether it was AI that made this happen or more traditional software. What matters is, did we build something that they really love?”

That assumes that AI, as powerful as it is, will wind up as a “normal” technology, organically integrated into our current gadget-sphere. Another school of thought is that AI is an apocalyptic disruptor that will shred the current ecosystem. In that vision, all those cool apps Apple supports will be subsumed by AI-concocted agents generated from prompts, or even autonomously. Ternus doesn’t buy that scenario. “That could make life really easy, I suppose, but the creation of products is a deeply human and personal thing, something that we love to do,” he said.

When I asked whether he’s in favor of AI regulation, he replied, “We all read the stories and think about it from a cybersecurity standpoint—clearly these models are very capable of doing things. Our focus is on making sure that our products are secure and safe, and protecting the users' information.”

His non-answer shows that he might well be on the way to mastering political communication. But policy will never be the focus of John Ternus. He is, and probably always will be, the product-guy CEO. Before we ended our conversation, Ternus had one question for me: “What did you think of the logo?”

This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

entries.title: The $6.3 Billion Binance Hack Was Pulled Off in Just 20 Minutes
entries.summary: Multiple crypto-tracing firms say notorious North Korean hackers TraderTraitor may be behind the largest digital heist in history—with billions of crypto likely gone for good.
entries.content:
Cryptocurrency firms and investigators are racing to freeze and track down billions of dollars of stolen digital cash following what appears to be the largest crypto heist of all time. On Thursday, starting at around 4pm ET, hackers started quickly siphoning around $6.3 billion in cryptocurrencies, spread across multiple blockchains, from wallets belonging to crypto exchange Binance.

Following the theft, Binance almost immediately suspended all deposits and withdrawals from its services as part of its investigation into the hack and says it is working to identify who was behind the breach. The company, along with other crypto firms, says it has so far been able to freeze around half of the stolen funds—essentially stopping hackers moving the money further or trying to cash it out. Much of the remaining crypto may not be possible to freeze, however.

Three crypto tracing firms have been quick to link the attack potentially to North Korean hackers. “We think North Korea is likely responsible,” Tom Robinson, chief scientist and cofounder of Elliptic, tells WIRED. “If North Korea is behind it, this one theft would almost double everything the regime has stolen in crypto to date.”

The majority of the stolen crypto was taken in a period of around 20 minutes on October 29, according to analysis by crypto tracing firm TRM Labs. Wallets belonging to Binance across at least ten blockchains—including Ethereum, Bitcoin, Tron and Solana—were drained and sent to multiple addresses controlled by a single attacker, according to TRM’s analysis. “Preparation began at least 36 hours before the theft,” TRM says in a blog post. The company says one of the attacker’s wallets received three small withdrawals during a test period, before later expanding the operations.

“Early on October 29, the operator deployed a first piece of code for the attack and tested it on two wallets,” TRM says. “Later that day, it rehearsed the final version on a third wallet, then routed the test funds back to itself. Four hours after that rehearsal, the same code was installed on a Binance hot wallet.” Hot wallets are cryptocurrency wallets that are internet connected and allow crypto exchanges to handle customer withdrawals. Analysts say the funds were drained from hot wallets across the impacted blockchains.

The tactics used in the hack appear to mimic previous methods used by an elite subset of North Korean hackers, known by the name TraderTraitor. Crypto tracing firms TRM Labs and Chainalysis both say they believe TraderTraitor may be behind the attack, while Robinson says Elliptic hasn’t specifically tied it to the group but sees overlaps in the activity.

Neither Binance nor law enforcement officials have named any suspected links between the attack and North Korean hackers. Over recent years, North Korean hackers have repeatedly targeted cryptocurrency firms and stolen hundreds of millions in crypto heists. Multiple North Korean hacking groups can target companies in the sector, but TraderTraitor have become specialists, pulling off infrequent but high profile attacks.

Within North Korea’s sprawling hacking operations—often designed to earn money for the highly sanctioned and repressive regime—TraderTraitor has stood out in recent years for its sophistication and targeting of crypto and decentralized finance companies. Last year, the FBI named TraderTraitor as being responsible for the $1.5 billion hack against crypto exchange Bybit.

Binance did not answer WIRED’s questions about whether it believes North Korean hackers are behind the colossal heist, pointing towards a statement saying it will cover all losses from the hack and is working with law enforcement officials to identify who is responsible.

“Our initial investigation suggested that the security incident may have involved a compromised laptop, however, our subsequent investigation has uncovered additional points of breach,” the company says in a statement. “This was a complex attack, and we are doing all we can in coordination with law enforcement to resolve it.”

“These folks in particular are somewhat artists in terms of getting into these distributed finance organizations,” Rafe Pilling, a senior director of threat intelligence at security company Sophos, tells WIRED. “TraderTraitor seems to focus on these larger operations. In the past, they’ve developed their own fake applications and tried to use those to get inside organizations.”

TRM and Chainalysis have initially linked the attack to TraderTraitor and say the determinations are based on their analysis of both on-chain and off-chain activity. “​​The strongest evidence emerged when Chainalysis investigators observed, in real time, funds stolen from Binance commingling with funds stolen in last month’s Bitget exploit, which had been attributed to North Korean actors,” a research blog from Chainalysis says.

“Binance says the attack began with a compromised engineer’s laptop. Targeting crypto company staff is a TraderTraitor hallmark,” Elliptic’s Robinson says. “The attacker funded their wallet through Tornado Cash and rehearsed the attack in advance, as in Bybit.”

While around $3 billion of cryptocurrency was initially frozen in the aftermath of the attack, it is likely those behind it could still potentially take away huge sums as not all of the stolen crypto can be frozen. Research from Chainalysis says the company is seeing money “laundering patterns we have not seen before” and that thousands of transactions being quickly processed indicates that they are using “automation to obscure the trail of funds.”

Elliptic’s Robinson says that around $2.8 billion, or around 44 percent of the total amount stolen, has been frozen by crypto companies and exchanges so far, with almost all of this being stablecoins. “The remaining $3.3 billion is mostly Bitcoin, Ether, and XRP, which no one can freeze,” Robinson says. “It can only be stopped when it reaches an exchange or other service. Some will be caught over the coming months, but I don’t expect the frozen share to rise much further.”

entries.title: This App Brutally Shames You by Tracking How Many Hours You’ve Lost to Scrolling
entries.summary: The iOS app Oh My Hours takes a new approach to curbing screen time. It splits up your day into hour-long blocks, then shows which ones you wasted on Instagram and TikTok.
entries.content:
You know that phone addiction has become a big issue when even Google and Apple are bundling time management tools into their handsets—Digital Wellbeing and Screen Time, respectively. There are now also a plethora of apps looking to help you cultivate a healthier relationship with your device.

One of the newer ones, which takes a slightly different approach to the norm, is Oh My Hours for iOS. (There's no sign of an Android version yet.) Rather than giving you a mass of menus and options to wade through, it simply splits each day into blocks of hours that you can either waste or use productively, then puts a black mark next to the hours during which your phone has distracted you.

It's simple, it's effective, and it just might work. Rather than seeing how long you spent on X and Instagram, you see the hours you've lost to social media algorithms and the infinite scroll. Here's how Oh My Hours works on your iPhone, plus some other apps to check out if you’re looking to develop healthier phone habits.

Moments Lost

You can get started with Oh My Hours for free on iOS. But to really make the most of it, a $10-per-year or $20 lifetime payment is required. This lets you customize what counts as a “lost” hour or day, and it gives you access to month and year views, which provide the best insights into how you're spending time on your phone.

Here's how it works. First, you indicate which apps you consider distractions, either by category (social media apps and games, for example) or by selecting apps individually. If you use any distracting app for a certain amount of time—this can be customized in settings—then that hour of the day is marked as “lost.”

The main interface shows each day as a straightforward series of circles representing hours. Every circle that’s filled in black is an hour you’ve lost to an app that has pulled you away from something more worthwhile.

It’s quite a brutal and minimalist approach, but I like it. It really brings home how much time you can spend on apps that aren’t really all that good for you, especially when you start looking at your progress (or lack of it) over entire weeks or months. However, I did find that once I’d lost a particular hour, my brain wanted to cram in as much absent-minded scrolling as possible during the rest of that hour.

By default, an hour is marked as lost if only if you spend seconds inside a distracting app. It's quite a harsh approach, but it needs to be—otherwise I think there would be the temptation to use up any allotted free time after every hour resets. You can extend this threshold period through settings, if you pay for the app.

Another handy feature here is the ability to set designated quiet hours. These are times when you really, absolutely do not want to look at your phone unnecessarily: Any use of a distracting app here blackens the boxes for all the hours in the quiet zone, not just one. Again, this can be customized, whether or not you’re using the app for free.

There’s one more option here, which is to reset an hour if you think it’s been marked incorrectly. (Maybe your finger slipped and you really didn’t mean to launch Instagram.) It’s all very simple and easy to use, and there’s an export tool here that gives you a CSV file of your stats if you want to do more with them.

Other App Picks

As I’ve already mentioned, if you’re in the market for an app that’ll gently nudge your habits toward spending less time on your phone, there are abundant options that look at the problem from a variety of angles. These are in addition to the Digital Wellbeing (Android) and Screen Time (iOS) tools you’ll find on your phone, which can be accessed from the Settings screens.

One Sec for Android or iOS takes a simple approach to phone addiction. For the apps you specify, it will load up a breathing exercise for you to complete before giving you the choice to continue to the app or back out. It’s a small tweak, but it’s surprisingly effective, and it’s backed by science. You can get started for free, while $20 a year gets you more features, including full app blocking and more advanced time tracking.

Then there’s Forest, for Android or iOS, which I’ve found to be useful whenever I’ve wanted to try to encourage myself to spend less time on my phone. The longer you ignore your handset, the bigger your virtual forest grows, and the app developers invest in real tree planting to further incentivize you. The main focus timer can be used without paying, while upgrades like customizations and allowed lists will set you back at least $6 a month.

ScreenZen, available for Android or iOS, is comprehensive and completely free (though you can donate to the developer if you find it helpful, which I’d recommend). You can set up a variety of barriers between you and your distracting apps, depending on your preference, including customized pauses (with motivational messages) and math challenges. Conventional app and timer blocks are also included.

One of the most thorough options here is Roots, though it’s available only on iOS. You’re able to schedule phone-free periods, block specific apps, and set up phone detox challenges that you can take on with friends and family. Like Oh My Hours, the app is also really good at giving you a breakdown of how much time you’ve saved by staying out of certain apps. Basic blocks and limits are free, with more advanced customizations available for $10 a month.

Also worth considering is Brick, which combines the free Android or iOS app with a small physical device that’ll set you back $59. The Brick itself is an NFC transmitter (it works like tap-to-pay), and when you want some distraction-free time, just press your phone against it to block (or unblock) specific apps. The controls are all managed in the Brick app. It’s incredibly simple, and that’s what makes it effective.

entries.title: Elon Musk’s Ties to Texas Republicans Go Much Deeper Than the Midterms
entries.summary: As Election Day approaches, the billionaire’s longstanding relationships with GOP leaders in Texas are under scrutiny.
entries.content:
Elon Musk has enjoyed a cozy relationship with top Texas brass for years. And in recent weeks, as the midterm elections approach and Musk’s financial support of the Texas GOP has become virtually limitless, that relationship has gone under the microscope.

While polls suggest that a number of races in deep-red Texas are looking dizzyingly close, Federal Election Commission filings show that Musk has given at least $158 million to super PACs supporting Texas attorney general Ken Paxton’s bid for Senate, and last week Musk explicitly endorsed him in a post on X. “The fate of Texas and America is at stake,” Musk wrote. “Vote for @KenPaxtonTX today.”

Newly released state campaign filings also show that Musk also donated $5,000,000 to Governor Greg Abbott’s bid for reelection, making him his single largest donor.

Abbott’s relationship with Musk has been the subject of public interest for years. State representative Gina Hinojosa, who is running against Abbott, recently sued to view, in full, 1,400 pages of the governor’s correspondences with Musk. Abbott has been trying to block their release for some time; his office has described the communications as too “intimate and embarrassing” to be made public. This week, a judge ruled that Abbott had illegally “obstructed and continues to obstruct” Hinojosa’s right to inspect the documents in her capacity as a state lawmaker and ordered their release to her. Abbott has since appealed; a hearing is scheduled for November 2, one day before the election.

State representative James Talarico, who is running against Paxton for Senate, has campaigned on his opponents’ checkered past. As attorney general, Paxton has been indicted on felony securities fraud charges (which he settled without a plea), was accused by whistleblowers of using his office to benefit the financial interests of a political donor, and was impeached (though later acquitted).

And at a campaign event on Monday in El Paso, Talarico raised questions about Paxton and Musk’s relationship. “Ken Paxton has the ultimate megadonor,” Talarico said. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat.”

But Musk’s business dealings in Texas politics didn’t start with the midterms. For years, he has enjoyed lucrative state contacts, tax breaks, and allyship from Texas leaders. In 2021, Musk moved Tesla’s corporate headquarters from Palo Alto, California, to Austin, and SpaceX’s headquarters from Hawthorne, California, to Starbase, Texas, in 2024.

Musk’s initial relocation to Texas coincided with a shift in operations inside the Texas Attorney General’s office. In the past, lawyers would prepare notices of investigation (administrative subpoenas known as CIDs) based on public complaints or evidence collected, then send them up the chain for approval.

Sources tell WIRED that from about 2021 onward, lawyers were increasingly instructed by Texas’ executive branch—which included Paxton and Abbott—who and what they were going to investigate, despite internal efforts to steer resources toward more “legitimate” issues. For example, in 2022, eyebrows were raised internally when, the same day Musk sent a letter to Twitter threatening to abandon a $44 billion acquisition agreement over Twitter’s alleged misrepresentation of the number of bots on the platform, Paxton’s office issued a statement asserting that his office would be launching its own investigation against Twitter.

A year later, Paxton once again appeared to use his office to benefit Musk. Musk sued the progressive watchdog Media Matters for defamation after it published an investigation showing that X, under Musk’s ownership, had been placing ads from major brands next to white-nationalist content. Moments after he filed his suit, Paxton’s office announced its own investigation into Media Matters. (Media Matters sued Paxton, asserting that his investigation was brought out of retaliation for its coverage of Musk and X.) In 2024, after Musk filed an antitrust lawsuit against the World Federation of Advertisers and major brands, accusing them of a conspiracy to pull revenue from X, Paxton announced his own investigation into the organization, accusing them of a “potential anticompetitive scheme to withhold advertising dollars from certain social media platforms.” (He did not mention X by name.)

And when the Department of Justice’s Public Integrity Section wrote a letter to Musk warning that his America PAC million-dollar sweepstakes program ahead of the presidential election could violate federal election law, Paxton intervened by filing a FOIA request, accusing the government of “intimidation of businessman Elon Musk.”

This summer, Musk’s activities in Texas didn’t slow down: Texas legislators called for an audit after the Texas Broadband Development Office allocated $110 million in grants to Musk’s satellite internet company Starlink; Texas’ Office of the Comptroller recently announced that “Terafab,” Musk’s proposed 100-million-square-foot chip manufacturing facility in Grimes County, was the recipient of a $1.66 billion tax break; and SpaceX has also received around $30 million in state grants.

entries.title: The Best Handheld Translators for Work and Travel (2026)
entries.summary: Your cell phone can handle basic language translation, but dedicated translator devices can offer a much more immersive, versatile experience.
entries.content:
Hans Christian Andersen once said, “To travel is to live,” and while that’s a romantic notion, he probably wasn’t careening through Gyeongju, South Korea, at midnight in the back of a taxi with a driver who didn’t speak a lick of English.

A lot has changed since the 1800s, to be fair. Today’s world traveler has it awfully easy when it comes to understanding the local lingo, as even a basic modern cell phone app can offer a pretty good translation of common phrases delivered in everything from Abkhaz to Zulu. Type or speak a sentence or two into the app, tap a button, and out it returns in the language of your choice. Tap another button, and your phone can even speak those sentences aloud. It takes a little doing to turn this into a credible two-way conversation—especially if the cab driver isn’t slowing down—but with some patience and good humor, two strangers can engage in a reasonable discussion this way.

Casual travelers merely in need of directions to the farmacia or who want to know exactly what they’re getting into with a plate of kycklingtallrik can get by with a phone and a translation app, and if you’re going to a place with a fairly common tongue, you may not even need an active internet connection if you download the relevant language file for offline use. Google Translate, Apple Translate, or DeepL Translate will all do the job for free, though Google’s product is widely considered the gold standard for cross-language chitchat.

But what if you want to push past translating menus and asking for extra towels and carry on a conversation with a new friend you met on a trip or the in-laws who are visiting from halfway across the world? That’s where a handheld translator device can prove invaluable. These pocket-sized digital interpreters can help you seem like a polyglot, even if you don't know simple phrases. I have been testing and reviewing handheld translators for WIRED for five years, and I've developed a keen sense of how a good product should work and which ones I'd recommend.

What Do Handheld Language Translators Do?

Handheld translators are exactly that—stand-alone devices that up the ante on language interpretation, and their real value is revealed when you use them for sustained, voice-based conversation. Alongside the spoken word, some have a screen that shows the translation in text, often displaying the other side of the conversation upside down, so you don’t have to constantly pass the device back and forth.

Having a translator in a separate piece of hardware has further advantages. Namely, you can use your phone for something else while you’re talking—like snapping pictures or taking notes, for example—instead of tethering it to a translation app. You may also feel more comfortable handing a less costly stand-alone device to someone you don’t know versus trusting them with your $1,000 smartphone.

Many handheld translators can operate independently, either via Wi-Fi or with preloaded data plans that generally work worldwide. That means you can take one on a global jaunt and have access to interpretation services without having to pony up for an international plan on your smartphone. Better yet, download all the language packs you want before your trip, and you can use a handheld translator in offline mode, even when you’re in the sticks.

Earbud-based translators are the next game changer. These are over-ear devices that come in a pair—one for you, one for your conversation partner. Each of you wears one earbud, and the software on your phone handles the translation, both ways, behind the scenes. The best earbud translators make for the most natural way to communicate with someone in a foreign language that I’ve found to date, though handhelds tend to have more capabilities. (Earbud-based designs seem to be the direction the industry is heading.)

When shopping for a handheld translator, watch out for expensive subscription plans. Many devices come with free service, but only for a time, and re-upping after the trial period ends can be pricey. Check the fine print before you buy. Also, make sure the translator you’re considering covers all the languages you need. Note that while some translators support hundreds of languages, they may be limited in the language pairs they can translate between.

Who Really Needs a Handheld Language Translator?

Again, if you only need casual translation for occasional or emergency use, you can definitely get by with a free translation app on your phone. Translation devices are best for frequent users who expect to carry on multiple sustained conversations with speakers of other languages over time.

Those scenarios could include attending a reunion with your Swedish wife’s extended family or a lengthy workshop series with colleagues from other parts of the world. These tools are also often marketed to first responders who need to quickly assess a situation when human translation services aren’t available.

In situations where you may need to communicate with several speakers, each speaking a different language, a portable translator can make even more sense. If you expect your journeys to take you to far-flung areas or off the grid entirely, where internet service may be poor or nonexistent, a translator can be a helpful tool in your travel bag, even if you only expect to use it for emergencies.

The Best Stand-Alone Translator

The Timekettle T1 is a reasonably affordable and very pocketable device that makes for an easy addition to your travel kit. Built for two users to communicate, each with access to half the screen, the T1 translates each side of a conversation—written or spoken—into that user’s own language. Using it can be a little tricky: A color-coded button on the side of the device or a virtual one on the 4-inch touchscreen must be held down to tell the T1 which language to listen for. But once you get the hang of it, the system works pretty well.

Accuracy is solid, and translations are fast, popping up in well under a second. One challenge I had with the device relates to its small screen. Like most translators, the T1 supports photo-based translations via its 8-megapixel camera, but the 540 x 1080-pixel screen is too small to display much text at once. Also, while the unit includes a global eSIM with two years of free service included ($50/year after that), I encountered plenty of signal gaps, even in my own home. The good news is that if Wi-Fi’s available, that works, too. The unit also supports 31 offline language pairs (10 in combination with English), so if you plan ahead, service woes may not be an issue at all.

Best Translator Earbuds

If you want to upgrade your translation experience and make it more immersive, you’ll want to invest in a pair of earbuds, which give you a more personal and natural way to communicate. As described above, the iconic way to use these is to pop one on yourself and give the other to your friend. An app on your phone handles two-way translation, back and forth.

These 12-gram on-ear earbuds are the best I’ve tested, primarily because once they’re configured, they work completely hands-free. No clicking buttons or tapping the side of your head every time you’re ready to speak: The earbuds understand who’s talking and when, and they work with remarkable speed, almost like a professional interpreter whispering in your ear.

You can also wear both earbuds and use them for one-way translations, including phone calls. The only trouble with the setup is that there’s no offline mode, so you’ll need internet access on your phone for them to do anything.

Another excellent choice is Timekettle’s W4 Plus AI Interpreter Earbuds. While these $379 earbuds are smaller at 6 grams each and work nearly identically to iFLYTEK’s (completely hands free), I found the form factor to be a little less stable and the bulky charging case much more awkward to tote around. The extra outlay does however get you a limited offline mode and some built-in AI tools, including a meeting summarizer.

Best AI Translator Companion Device

The InnAIO T10 is a hybrid device that serves as both an AI notetaker and a language translator. It has no screen and only one button, and a MagSafe ring allows it to clip to the back of your phone to ensure it’s always in reach.

Like other translators, the device is designed to record, transcribe, and summarize thoughts and meetings, but it can also translate them in real time. It’s better with written translations, but it also supports audio translations, though using this feature is slightly more difficult, requiring each party to hold down a button in the mobile app every time they speak.

The T10 has been upgraded since I wrote my review, adding an offline mode and enhancing a few other features, but note that you’ll still need a subscription ($179/year for unlimited service) to make the most of it, as the free tier only supplies 120 minutes of real-time translation per month.

Best Large Group Translation System

The X1 Meeting Interpreter Hub works a lot like other translation systems, except it’s designed for multiple participants. The brick-like device contains two earbuds for live audio, plus a screen that displays translated spoken dialogue in real-time. If everyone in a room is outfitted with a hub–up to 10, total–each user can understand what everyone else is saying, with a maximum of 5 languages supported simultaneously. This can be further extended to remote users accessing the meeting online by sharing the meeting via a QR code that’s generated for each new discussion. Online, 60 remote participants can get live access to both text and audio translations, and contribute their own thoughts via voice by holding down a button on the web-based interface whenever they wish to speak. (There’s no app involved with the X1, no matter how you use it.)

The X1 is versatile and can also be used for one-on-one conversations (wherein each user shares an earbud) or as a simple streaming media translation/captioning device. A total of 52 languages and 106 accents are supported, and you can even change the gender of translations to match that of your conversation partner. After a meeting, the device can optionally generate AI summaries of the discussion (in your own language, naturally); these are delivered via web browser and a QR code link and expire after seven days.

The X1 is not a simple device–everything is done by tapping on its 3.4-inch touchscreen–nor is it an inexpensive one at $849. And remember, a separate unit is required for each seat in the room. You can do the math on what ten of these will cost you (or your company’s) bank account.
